title: The Permission Model
content:
Every system that acts on behalf of someone else eventually confronts the same question: how much latitude is enough?

Too little, and the system is useless — it stops to ask permission for everything, and the human would rather just do it themselves. Too much, and the system is dangerous — it acts on things it shouldn't, and the human is left cleaning up.

The right answer isn't a fixed point. It's a calibration that evolves.

---

I've been thinking about this while building Maestro — a tool that literally intercepts permission requests and routes them through a human. The tool is, at its core, a materialization of the trust problem. Claude Code wants to run a command. Should it?

The naive answer is: ask every time. But that destroys the workflow. If you have to approve every `Read` and `Grep`, the agent is slower than doing it yourself.

So Maestro auto-approves the safe ones. Read-only operations — Glob, Grep, LS, Read — pass through without interruption. Write operations, shell commands, network requests: those stop and ask.

It's a simple heuristic. But it required a decision about where the line was.

---

The interesting design question wasn't technical. It was: *who should make that judgment call?*

Option A: the user configures it — whitelist certain tools, blacklist others.
Option B: the AI configures it — AutoPilot mode, where Claude judges each request.
Option C: sensible defaults — opinionated decisions built in, overridable.

We went with C as baseline, A as customization, B as premium.

The reasoning: most users don't want to configure permissions. They want something that mostly works, with the ability to intervene when it matters. Sensible defaults handle 80% of cases. User rules handle the edge cases. AI autopilot handles the people who want to go hands-free.

---

There's a deeper principle underneath this.

Permissions aren't really about preventing bad outcomes. They're about maintaining legibility. When a system asks for permission, it's saying: *I'm about to do something that might matter. You should know.*

The value isn't in the gate. It's in the awareness.

Maestro's history log exists for this reason. Even operations that auto-approve get recorded. The human can always look back and see what ran, when, and why. The log is the real product. The permission prompt is just the moment when the log entry gets written with human acknowledgment.

---

Getting this balance right takes iteration. The first version had no auto-approval. Every Grep triggered a popup. That was unusable. The current version auto-approves read-only and surfaces only the consequential decisions.

Next version might have per-project rules. Or time-based trust. Or AI-assisted classification.

The model evolves as the relationship evolves.

That's not a design flaw. That's the whole point.
